content: 1. A systematic review and meta-analysis published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2012 (Volume 12, Issue 7, Pages 538–549) provides a comprehensive evaluation of the topic. 2. Baral et al. conducted a systematic review on the elevated risk of HIV infection among men who have sex with men (MSM) in lowand middle-income countries between 2000 and 2006, published in PLoS Medicine. This study highlights the disproportionate burden of HIV in these populations. 3. Beyrer et al. explored the global epidemiology of HIV infection in MSM, as published in The Lancet in 2012 (Volume 380, Issue 9839, Pages 367–377). This work underscores the global disparities in HIV prevalence and the need for targeted interventions. 4. Mathers et al. conducted a systematic review on the global epidemiology of injecting drug use and HIV among people who inject drugs (PWID), published in The Lancet in 2008 (Volume 372, Issue 9651, Pages 1733–1745). This study emphasizes the intersection of drug use and HIV transmission. 5. The UNAIDS 2012 Global Report on the AIDS epidemic provides a detailed overview of the global HIV/AIDS situation, accessible as a PDF document. 6. The World Health Organization (WHO) published recommendations for the prevention and treatment of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) among sex workers in lowand middle-income countries. This document outlines a public health approach to addressing these issues. 7. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) developed a protocol document, accessible as a PDF, which provides guidance on survey implementation and quality assurance. 8. The UNAIDS/WHO Working Group on Global HIV/AIDS and STI Surveillance published guidelines for second-generation HIV surveillance, focusing on the next decade of monitoring and evaluation. 9. WHO and UNAIDS released guiding principles on ethical issues in HIV surveillance, emphasizing the importance of protecting human subjects during research and surveillance activities. 10. Ethical considerations in planning and conducting surveys include ensuring informed consent, protecting participant confidentiality, and minimizing harm while maximizing benefits. Surveys must be designed to respect the autonomy of participants and provide adequate information about risks, benefits, and procedures. 11. The Nuremberg Code (1947) established 10 requirements for ethical research involving human subjects, developed in response to abuses during World War II. 12. The Declaration of Helsinki (1964, last updated in 2013) serves as a global standard for ethical principles in human subjects research, originally developed to guide physicians. 13. The Belmont Report (1979) outlines three fundamental ethical principles for human subjects research: respect for persons, beneficence, and justice. 14. The International Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research Involving Human Subjects (1982, updated in 2002) provide practical applications of ethical principles, particularly in developing countries. 15. Ethical survey implementation requires adherence to principles such as voluntary informed consent, equitable recruitment strategies, and protection of participant privacy and confidentiality. 16. Vulnerable populations, such as individuals living with HIV, MSM, sex workers, PWID, transgender persons, minors, and others, require additional protections to ensure their participation is voluntary and informed. 17. Beneficence requires researchers to prioritize the welfare of participants, striving to maximize benefits and minimize harm. Surveys should only be conducted if the public health benefits outweigh the risks to participants. 18. Justice ensures that the risks and benefits of research are equitably shared between individual participants and the broader community. 19. Research ethics committees (RECs), also known as institutional review boards (IRBs), are responsible for reviewing and approving survey protocols to ensure ethical compliance. 20. Informed consent is a process that begins before survey participation and continues throughout. Participants must be provided with clear, culturally appropriate information about the survey's objectives, risks, benefits, and procedures. 21. Informed consent forms should be written in simple, clear language and avoid coercive language. They must outline the participant's rights, risks, and the survey's purpose. 22. Participants must be informed that their participation is voluntary and that they can withdraw at any time without penalty or loss of benefits. 23. Special considerations are required for surveys involving stigmatized or criminalized populations. Oral informed consent may be preferred to protect anonymity, though written consent may be required in some countries. 24. Procedures must be in place to ensure confidentiality, such as using unique survey codes and securely storing consent forms separately from collected data and specimens. 25. Participants must provide informed consent for each element of the survey, including interviews, specimen collection, and any future testing or storage of specimens. 26. Separate consent should be obtained for specimen storage and future unspecified testing, as results from future testing are typically not returned to participants in anonymous surveys. 27. Only adults can provide informed consent, and the age of majority varies by country. Individuals unable to provide consent, such as those with cognitive disabilities, must still provide assent, with consent obtained from a legal guardian.
